claim: Two-thirds of human hormones act on membrane receptors that couple to G proteins.
source: Two-thirds of human hormones and one-third of clinical drugs act on membrane receptors that couple to G proteins to achieve appropriate functional responses.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract without specific citation, drawing from general scientific knowledge.

evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of the three datasets presented in the manuscript.

claim: GPCRs represent the largest family of proteins involved in signal propagation across biological membranes.

evidence: This is stated as established scientific knowledge and is supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2020.

claim: GPCRs recognize signals ranging from photons and odors to neurotransmitters, hormones, and cytokines.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Armstrong et al., 2020.

claim: G proteins are heterotrimeric proteins consisting of α, β, and γ subunits.
source: G proteins are heterotrimeric proteins consisting of α, β, and γ subunits that dissociate to α and βγ upon activation by a GPCR.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about G protein structure.

claim: G proteins dissociate to α and βγ subunits upon activation by a GPCR.

claim: There are 16 human G protein α subunits.

claim: The Inoue group determined coupling profiles of 148 GPCRs to the Gq wildtype and 10 G protein chimeras.

claim: The Inoue dataset includes NTS1 and TRH1 receptors not included in the previous publication, making it 150 receptors total.

claim: The Inoue group used chimeras consisting of a Gq backbone in which the six most C-terminal Gα residues have been replaced to represent all 16 human G proteins.

claim: Five of the Inoue chimeras have identical sequences to other G proteins.

claim: Aggregation of G proteins onto families based on maximum subtype values gives the best comparability.

evidence: This is based on analysis comparing different aggregation methods.
